evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(txt, at), MA(RATIO(txt, at), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a firm's tax expense drops far below its own historical level while its accruals are high, book income is diverging from taxable income — the classic signature of earnings management that carries no tax cost — and it simultaneously reveals that real taxable profitability has evaporated.
evaluated.reasoning: Book-tax divergence is the one accounting-quality channel the archive has never tested, and it is a genuine interaction: high accruals plus a normal tax bill means the earnings are being taxed and hence probably real, while high accruals plus a collapsed tax bill means they are not. Using the deviation from the firm's own five-year tax intensity rather than a tax-rate level avoids the near-zero-denominator problems of effective-tax-rate measures and keeps the conditioner distinct from a profitability sort.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithLiquidityBelowIndustryNorm
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(che, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash needs are industry-determined — a software firm and a grocer require very different buffers — so the fragility that matters is holding *less* cash against liabilities than peers, and that is where unconverted accruals must be resolved through forced action rather than waited out.
evaluated.reasoning: The industry-relative framing was the single most successful conditioner design in the archive on the leverage dimension, while absolute liquidity measures (che/lct, che/lt, cash-flow coverage) were mediocre or failed; this tests whether the improvement comes from the peer benchmarking itself rather than from leverage specifically. If it works, the lesson generalises to a design principle rather than a single variable choice.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReceivableAccrualsWithExcessIndustryLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(NEG(recch), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Receivable build-up is the accrual component whose reversal runs through bad-debt provisions, and it is punished in firms carrying more debt than their industry peers, who cannot fund a collection shortfall the way a normally financed competitor can.
evaluated.reasoning: The component leg (−5.4%, t −3.72) and the peer-relative conditioner (−4.7%, t −3.48) are the archive's two strongest ingredients and both were obtained with different partners, so this is a real independence test rather than a redundant recombination — and unlike its predecessor it uses a conditioner that carries no cross-sectional distress premium. Coverage near 0.075 is the main risk and should be weighed before treating any improvement as evidence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsAsDebtMigratesToShortTerm
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dltt, lt), MA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 5)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A fall in the long-term share of liabilities below the firm's own norm means debt has been reclassified as current — maturities approaching without refinancing, or covenant breaches accelerating obligations — so accrued earnings must convert to cash on a compressed schedule.
evaluated.reasoning: This is economically distinct from the rollover-funding signal that worked (−3.5%, t −2.69): that measured *new* short-term borrowing, whereas maturity migration requires no new financing and captures the involuntary shortening that precedes default. It also keeps the successful "deviation from own norm" design while changing the balance-sheet dimension being benchmarked.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithIdiosyncraticLeverageDeterioration
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Leverage rises for two very different reasons — sector-wide credit cycles that lift everyone's debt ratios, and firm-specific deterioration — and only the idiosyncratic component signals that this particular firm is losing financial flexibility, which is when its unconverted accruals become a problem.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the *change* in leverage is not a blend of the two evaluated conditioners: the own-norm measure leaves sector credit cycles in (so it flags whole industries at once) and the peer-level measure captures a static capital-structure position, whereas this isolates firm-specific deterioration in the current year. That distinction is economically substantive, and purging the common component should also reduce the cross-sectional clustering that plausibly weakened Fama-MacBeth slopes in this family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithExcessDebtPerRevenueDollar
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, sale))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Obligations are ultimately serviced out of revenue, not out of book assets, so the fragile firms are those carrying more liabilities per dollar of sales than their industry peers — asset-heavy or asset-light borrowers with too thin a revenue base — and accrual reversals there translate into refinancing problems rather than mere earnings misses.
evaluated.reasoning: This removes the contamination the critic identified: the conditioner contains no earnings variable at all (no pi, ib, dp or oancf), so it cannot reduce to accruals interacted with industry-adjusted profitability, and it is a genuinely different scaling of the debt burden than lt/at. Debt-to-revenue is a standard credit-analysis ratio that discriminates precisely among the firms lt/at treats as identical — those with the same balance-sheet leverage but very different revenue capacity to service it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithSalesGrowthBelowIndustry
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Losing revenue while your industry grows is firm-specific demand deterioration — share loss, product obsolescence, customers defecting — and receivables and inventory accrued against that shrinking franchise will be collected or sold only at a discount.
evaluated.reasoning: Revenue decline was the conditioner behind the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope, but it was measured in raw or within-firm form and so conflated industry downturns with firm-specific failure; industry-demeaning isolates the idiosyncratic component, which is the same transformation that lifted the leverage conditioner from −4.1% to −4.7% with the best Sharpe in the archive. It also avoids the Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny sales-growth premium being a sector bet, since the conditioner is demeaned within industry.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsUnderUnstableCapitalStructure
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(lt, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms whose leverage ratio swings from year to year lack a stable financing plan — they borrow when cash runs short and repay when it does not — and such firms cannot commit funding to carry the working capital their accruals represent.
evaluated.reasoning: Every distress conditioner in the archive is a level, a deterioration or a peer gap; second-moment financial instability is a distinct state that can be high even for moderately levered firms, so it is not a rescaling of any tested measure. If it works, it says the interaction is about financing *unreliability* rather than the amount of debt, which would materially change the economic interpretation of the whole family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithExcessSupplierFinancingVsPeers
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), sale))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Non-debt current liabilities — payables and accrued expenses — are involuntary financing: a firm carrying more of them per dollar of sales than its industry peers is stretching suppliers and deferring obligations because cheaper funding is unavailable, and it is in no position to carry accrued but uncollected earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: All distress dimensions tested so far are on the debt or equity side; trade-credit dependence is a distinct, non-market form of financial pressure that shows up before debt ratios move, and scaling by sales makes it comparable across firms while industry demeaning removes the large sectoral differences in payment terms. It uses no earnings variable in the conditioner, so it cannot reduce to accruals interacted with profitability — the flaw that invalidated the earlier debt-service-capacity attempt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithConvexDistressThreshold
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), ADD(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))), INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0.15)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress costs are convex, not linear: being slightly more levered than peers is manageable, but once leverage exceeds the industry norm by a material margin the firm enters the region where covenants bind, lenders demand cash and accrual reversals must be settled immediately rather than absorbed.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a functional-form hypothesis about firms rather than an estimator swap: adding a kink at 15 percentage points of excess leverage tests whether the accrual-fragility interaction is threshold-driven, which is the economic explanation for the family's pattern of strong decile alphas alongside weak linear slopes. Unlike the earlier indicator gate that destroyed the alpha by zeroing half the cross-section, every firm retains its rank-based weight, so the portfolio tails stay populated while the slope gains the extra curvature.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsPerUnitOfLossAbsorbingCapital
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is the size of the accrual relative to the capital that must absorb its reversal: the same accrual-to-assets figure is trivial for a firm with a thick equity cushion and existential for one whose book equity has been eroded, so accruals scaled by loss-absorbing capital is itself the interaction.
evaluated.reasoning: Arithmetically this equals the accrual-to-assets ratio multiplied by the assets-to-equity leverage factor, so the fragility amplification is continuous and unbounded in the *level* of leverage rather than compressed into a [0,1] rank — a structurally different design from the ten multiplicative variants in the archive and the one most likely to produce a strong cross-sectional slope, since the amplification no longer discards magnitude information. Flooring the denominator at cash holdings keeps it positive for firms with negative or near-zero book equity, so the sign is well defined precisely where distress is most severe, and winsorising controls the remaining scale.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithProductMarketAndFinancialWeakness
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))), IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that is losing revenue share to its peers *and* carrying more debt than they do faces fragility on two independent fronts — it cannot grow out of its accrued working capital and cannot refinance around it — so its accrual reversals are the least likely to be absorbed.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the collinear leverage blend the critic rejected, product-market decline and financial over-extension are conceptually and empirically distinct dimensions, and each independently produced the archive's strongest evidence in its own metric (sales gap: fmb −2.03; leverage gap: α −4.7%, t −3.48). Both legs are industry-demeaned, so neither the sector composition of leverage nor an industry-wide demand shock can drive the sort, and the SUMRANK multiplier stays smooth so the cross-sectional slope is not degraded.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithDemandLoss
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The damage from an accrual reversal is its size relative to the equity that must absorb it, and its likelihood is highest when the firm is losing revenue to peers, so the two should be measured multiplicatively: accrual per dollar of loss-absorbing capital, amplified by idiosyncratic demand loss.
evaluated.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two structurally different innovations — continuous, unbounded fragility scaling through the equity-cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, Sharpe −0.456) and the best-performing peer-relative conditioner — rather than adding a twelfth rank multiplier to the same asset-deflated accrual. If the combination beats both parents, it establishes that magnitude scaling and conditional amplification capture different aspects of fragility, which is the key open question for the final generation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithVolatileRevenueBase
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(sale, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility can be operating rather than financial: a firm whose revenue base swings unpredictably cannot forecast the collections and inventory turnover its accruals presume, so accrued earnings in such firms are systematically less likely to convert to cash.
evaluated.reasoning: Leverage volatility worked as a second-moment conditioner (α −4.1%, t −3.03) but plausibly proxied for restructuring activity; revenue volatility isolates business risk with no financing content and shares no variable with the accrual leg, so it discriminates between the two interpretations of that result. It is the only untested fragility dimension that is a genuine second moment of the operating business.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BalanceSheetAccrualsWithDemandLoss
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Balance-sheet working-capital accruals are informative specifically when demand is deteriorating — that is when a rise in receivables and inventory cannot be explained by growth — which would explain why this accrual leg predicts correctly with revenue-based conditioners and perversely with financing-based ones.
evaluated.reasoning: The balance-sheet leg produced the archive's strongest slope with the within-firm revenue trough (fmb −3.63) but sign-flipped with chronic contraction (α +3.3%) and cash-flow coverage (α +0.7%), and this pins down whether the demand channel is what rescues it, using the conditioner form that has proven most reliable. It also carries the highest coverage in the archive (~0.10 versus 0.08), so a confirmation would give the final generation a broader-sample alternative to the cash-flow accrual leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithSlowCashConversionVsPeers
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(act, sale))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose current assets represent far more days of sales than its industry peers has a structurally slow cash conversion cycle, so accrued earnings sit in receivables and inventory for longer, are more exposed to obsolescence and non-collection, and cannot be turned into cash quickly when obligations fall due.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces a threshold transplant with a new fragility dimension — the length of the operating cycle relative to peers — which is an operating-liquidity constraint rather than any of the financing, demand, or second-moment dimensions already tested, and it is a *level* measure so it is not mechanically tied to the accrual change in the other leg. Industry-demeaning is essential here because cycle length is a sector technology, and it is the transformation that has consistently improved this family's cross-sectional slopes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsUnderWorstDimensionOfFragility
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), MAX(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financial fragility is determined by the binding constraint, not by an average: a firm that is severely over-levered relative to peers is fragile even if its revenue is growing, and a firm losing revenue share is fragile even at modest leverage, so the relevant amplifier of accrual risk is the *worst* of the two peer-relative dimensions.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a functional-form hypothesis about how distress dimensions aggregate, and MAX is a structure the archive has never used — it directly contrasts with the SUMRANK average of the same two dimensions, so the pair identifies whether fragility is additive or determined by a single binding constraint. Because MAX keeps a firm in the extreme portfolios when either dimension is extreme, the short leg should be populated by genuinely stressed firms rather than by moderate cases that score middling on both, which is the plausible reason averaging has capped this family's alpha near −4.7%.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DualEstimateAccrualsWithDemandLoss
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash-flow and balance-sheet accrual measures are two noisy estimates of the same economic quantity; their sum retains the common accrual signal while the estimation errors — articulation differences, mergers, reclassifications — partially cancel, so the extreme portfolios contain firms where both statements agree that accruals are extreme.
evaluated.reasoning: This directly repairs the sharpest anomaly in the archive: the balance-sheet leg with this conditioner gave fmb −3.90 but α −0.6%, exactly what happens when measurement noise widens cross-sectional dispersion without adding return information, while the cash-flow leg gave α −4.1% with fmb −2.03. Averaging the two estimates is an econometric fix with an economic justification, and it should inherit the slope strength of one leg and the portfolio strength of the other.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithBindingNonDebtPressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), MAX(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), sale))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financial pressure need not come from lenders: a firm financing itself with more payables and accrued expenses per sales dollar than its peers is already rationed, and combined with revenue share loss it is in the same weakest-link position as an over-levered firm.
evaluated.reasoning: Trade-credit dependence produced α −4.5% (t −3.61) as a standalone conditioner, close to peer leverage, so substituting it into the winning MAX structure tests whether the binding-constraint result is about debt specifically or about financing pressure generally — a substantive economic question, not a reshuffle. It also gives a robustness check on the gen-8 MAX finding using a conditioner drawn from an entirely different part of the balance sheet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithVolatileRevenue
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(sale, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility has a capacity dimension and an uncertainty dimension: a thin equity cushion determines how much of an accrual reversal the firm can absorb, while an unstable revenue base determines how likely the reversal is, so accruals scaled by loss-absorbing capital should be most damaging where revenue is least predictable.
evaluated.reasoning: Both ingredients worked independently through different channels — the cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, α −3.8%, Sharpe −0.456) and revenue-base volatility (fmb −1.65, α −3.7%) — and neither shares a variable with the other, so their combination tests whether absorption capacity and cash-flow uncertainty are complementary rather than duplicative descriptions of fragility. Unlike the peer-gap conditioners this pairing contains no growth or leverage term, so it provides an independent confirmation route for the family's central claim.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsCompositionAccrualsUnderExcessLeverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), dp)), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a fragile firm is not how large accruals are relative to its asset base but what fraction of its reported earnings is non-cash: when most of the earnings of an over-levered firm is accrual rather than cash, there is nothing available to service obligations and the reported profit will not survive.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the fragile MAX(ceq, che) deflator with a strictly positive, scale-free earnings-composition denominator (|ib| + dp), so it measures earnings *quality* rather than accrual size — economically distinct from every asset-deflated leg in the archive and free of the near-zero-equity outlier risk the critic identified. Combined with the peer-relative leverage gap, the best-performing single conditioner (α −4.7%, t −3.48), it asks whether cash-poor earnings composition is the channel through which leverage amplifies accruals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CountOfBindingFragilityFronts
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(che, lt))), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Fragility accumulates discretely: each front on which a firm is worse than its industry norm — more levered, losing revenue share, holding less cash — removes one escape route from an accrual reversal, so the number of failed fronts, not the worst one, measures how trapped the firm is.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the degeneracy the critic identified: a maximum of three cross-sectional ranks piles up near unity and becomes a near-constant multiplier, whereas a count of industry-median breaches is spread across 0–3 with substantial mass in each bucket, so the conditioning actually discriminates. It is also an Ohlson-style discrete distress score rather than another continuous rank transform, giving a genuinely different aggregation hypothesis than either MAX or averaging.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ChronicPeerExcessLeverageAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: One year of above-peer leverage can be a deliberate, reversible financing choice, but three consecutive years means the firm has been unable to deleverage and its debt capacity is exhausted, so accrual reversals must be absorbed by write-downs rather than by borrowing.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than twisting the aggregation operator on two known legs, this introduces persistence on the archive's strongest conditioning dimension — a state variable distinct from its level (tested), its one-year change (tested) and its volatility (tested) — and the 0–3 count is well spread rather than compressed toward an endpoint. The economic claim is falsifiable and sharp: if only chronic excess leverage matters, this should beat the one-year peer gap; if the effect is about fresh deterioration, it should be weaker.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalAccrualsFragilityAmplified
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(wcap, 1), dp), at), 1), SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet working-capital accruals are less sustainable when the firm is simultaneously levered and short of liquid working capital; the fragility rank acts as a continuous amplifier of the accrual signal's return predictability.
considered.reasoning: The signed accrual term preserves direction (positive accruals predict low returns) while the positive fragility multiplier scales its magnitude with distress, giving smooth amplification without zero-mass or sign flips. Fragile firms cannot fund receivable/inventory build-ups, so such accruals are more likely to reverse or be written down.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualInstabilityUnderDebtBurden
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 5)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dlc, dltt), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Unstable accruals indicate low accrual quality and discretionary smoothing/reversal cycles; this opacity is most costly to investors in debt-heavy firms where information risk about solvency is priced with a lag.
considered.reasoning: Accrual volatility captures accrual-quality risk that a single-year accrual level misses, and interacting it with the debt ratio targets firms where opaque accounting and default risk compound. Investors underreact to opaque accounting in levered firms, so returns underperform as the true cash position is revealed.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsAtLiquidityTrough
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(act, lct), 5))))
considered.hypothesis: High accruals are most dangerous when the firm's current ratio sits at the bottom of its own five-year history, i.e. liquidity is at a trough relative to its normal state, indicating a genuine funding squeeze rather than a stable low-liquidity business model.
considered.reasoning: TS_RANK provides a firm-relative distress state that controls for permanent industry/business-model differences in liquidity levels, sharpening the conditioning variable. Accrual-heavy earnings reported at a self-relative liquidity trough are the most likely to be reversed, so subsequent returns should be lowest.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualDistressCenteredInteraction
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dlc, dltt), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The slope of returns on accruals steepens with financial leverage: among debt-burdened firms, accrual-inflated earnings face covenant and refinancing incentives to manage numbers and harsher reversal consequences, while among unlevered, cash-rich firms accruals carry little information about future cash generation.
considered.reasoning: Both inputs are cross-sectionally demeaned before multiplication, so the product is by construction close to orthogonal to the Sloan accrual main effect and the leverage/distress main effect and loads on the cross-derivative instead. A negative slope means the accrual-return relation is more negative for high-leverage firms and flat-to-reversed for low-leverage firms, which is exactly the conditional-severity claim rather than a repackaged single-theme anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderRefinancingPressure
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual-heavy earnings are most dangerous when debt is concentrated at the short end and cash cannot cover current liabilities, because the firm must roll over obligations before non-cash earnings convert to cash, so the accrual signal should be amplified by near-term funding pressure rather than by scale.
considered.reasoning: The accrual measure keeps the standard total-assets deflator (no double-counted cash, no small-denominator instability), and the interaction enters as a strictly positive amplifier built from maturity structure and cash coverage of current liabilities—two distress dimensions distinct from leverage level or profitability. Accruals in firms facing an imminent rollover need are more likely to be reversed, written down, or resolved through dilutive financing, so returns should be lowest where a large positive accrual meets high refinancing pressure.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualBuildupWithSolvencyDeterioration
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1), 1), SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: A fresh increase in accruals that coincides with a rising liability-to-asset ratio and a shrinking working-capital cushion is the signature of earnings inflation during a funding squeeze, and predicts weaker subsequent returns than either flow alone.
considered.reasoning: The conditioner now contains only balance-sheet deterioration flows—leverage change and working-capital change—so no profitability level enters and results cannot be attributed to the profitability premium. The signed accrual change preserves the earnings-inflation direction while the positive deterioration rank scales it, isolating the accrual effect specifically in firms whose solvency is worsening at the same time.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsAtOwnLeverageHighWater
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), TS_RANK(RATIO(lt, at), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Distress that matters for accrual quality is a deterioration relative to the firm's own norm: accrual-inflated earnings reported when leverage sits at its five-year high reflect balance-sheet stress rather than a stable capital-structure policy.
considered.reasoning: TS_RANK is roughly uniform within firm, so the conditioner carries little unconditional cross-sectional return signal and cannot smuggle in the leverage main effect — the design the critic scored highest in gen 0, now with a legal accrual-exclusive input. It also tests whether firm-relative distress states beat cross-sectional distress levels as the conditioning variable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DepreciationUnderProvisionInFragileFirms
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, at), 1)), 1), SUMRANK(RATIO(dltt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Fragile firms manage earnings through the depreciation lever — extending asset lives or shifting mix to slow write-offs — so a falling depreciation intensity in firms with heavy long-term debt and a retained-earnings deficit indicates non-cash earnings support that will reverse.
considered.reasoning: This tests an accrual-quality channel that is entirely separate from working-capital accruals (an estimate/allocation lever rather than a receivable/inventory lever) and is only meaningful jointly with distress, since healthy firms have little motive to stretch asset lives. The Altman-style conditioner (long-term debt burden plus retained-earnings deficit) uses cumulative solvency state rather than current profitability, keeping the profitability premium out of the attribution.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderRefinancingPressure

considered.name: AccrualsAsDebtMigratesToShortTerm
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(SUB(RATIO(dltt, lt), MA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 5)))))
considered.hypothesis: A fall in the long-term share of liabilities below the firm's own norm means debt has been reclassified as current — maturities approaching without refinancing, or covenant breaches accelerating obligations — so accrued earnings must convert to cash on a compressed schedule.
considered.reasoning: This is economically distinct from the rollover-funding signal that worked (−3.5%, t −2.69): that measured *new* short-term borrowing, whereas maturity migration requires no new financing and captures the involuntary shortening that precedes default. It also keeps the successful "deviation from own norm" design while changing the balance-sheet dimension being benchmarked.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithIdiosyncraticLeverageDeterioration
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Leverage rises for two very different reasons — sector-wide credit cycles that lift everyone's debt ratios, and firm-specific deterioration — and only the idiosyncratic component signals that this particular firm is losing financial flexibility, which is when its unconverted accruals become a problem.
considered.reasoning: Industry-demeaning the *change* in leverage is not a blend of the two evaluated conditioners: the own-norm measure leaves sector credit cycles in (so it flags whole industries at once) and the peer-level measure captures a static capital-structure position, whereas this isolates firm-specific deterioration in the current year. That distinction is economically substantive, and purging the common component should also reduce the cross-sectional clustering that plausibly weakened Fama-MacBeth slopes in this family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithExcessDebtPerRevenueDollar
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, sale))))
considered.hypothesis: Obligations are ultimately serviced out of revenue, not out of book assets, so the fragile firms are those carrying more liabilities per dollar of sales than their industry peers — asset-heavy or asset-light borrowers with too thin a revenue base — and accrual reversals there translate into refinancing problems rather than mere earnings misses.
considered.reasoning: This removes the contamination the critic identified: the conditioner contains no earnings variable at all (no pi, ib, dp or oancf), so it cannot reduce to accruals interacted with industry-adjusted profitability, and it is a genuinely different scaling of the debt burden than lt/at. Debt-to-revenue is a standard credit-analysis ratio that discriminates precisely among the firms lt/at treats as identical — those with the same balance-sheet leverage but very different revenue capacity to service it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithSalesGrowthBelowIndustry
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Losing revenue while your industry grows is firm-specific demand deterioration — share loss, product obsolescence, customers defecting — and receivables and inventory accrued against that shrinking franchise will be collected or sold only at a discount.
considered.reasoning: Revenue decline was the conditioner behind the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope, but it was measured in raw or within-firm form and so conflated industry downturns with firm-specific failure; industry-demeaning isolates the idiosyncratic component, which is the same transformation that lifted the leverage conditioner from −4.1% to −4.7% with the best Sharpe in the archive. It also avoids the Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny sales-growth premium being a sector bet, since the conditioner is demeaned within industry.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderUnstableCapitalStructure
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(lt, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose leverage ratio swings from year to year lack a stable financing plan — they borrow when cash runs short and repay when it does not — and such firms cannot commit funding to carry the working capital their accruals represent.
considered.reasoning: Every distress conditioner in the archive is a level, a deterioration or a peer gap; second-moment financial instability is a distinct state that can be high even for moderately levered firms, so it is not a rescaling of any tested measure. If it works, it says the interaction is about financing *unreliability* rather than the amount of debt, which would materially change the economic interpretation of the whole family.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ReceivableAccrualsWhenCashCannotCoverCurrentDebts
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(NEG(recch), at), 1), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, lct))))
considered.hypothesis: The receivable channel works through immediate cash need rather than through solvency: a firm whose cash cannot cover current liabilities must convert receivables now, and if those receivables were manufactured by loosened credit terms it will instead take a provision.
considered.reasoning: This is an attribution test of a live puzzle — receivables with the combined levered-and-cash-poor conditioner gave α −5.4% (t −3.72) while receivables with peer-excess leverage gave α +0.6% — so isolating the liquidity half of that SUMRANK identifies which component carried the result. The answer determines whether future consolidation should pair component accruals with liquidity stress or abandon the component leg entirely.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithExcessSupplierFinancingVsPeers
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), sale))))
considered.hypothesis: Non-debt current liabilities — payables and accrued expenses — are involuntary financing: a firm carrying more of them per dollar of sales than its industry peers is stretching suppliers and deferring obligations because cheaper funding is unavailable, and it is in no position to carry accrued but uncollected earnings.
considered.reasoning: All distress dimensions tested so far are on the debt or equity side; trade-credit dependence is a distinct, non-market form of financial pressure that shows up before debt ratios move, and scaling by sales makes it comparable across firms while industry demeaning removes the large sectoral differences in payment terms. It uses no earnings variable in the conditioner, so it cannot reduce to accruals interacted with profitability — the flaw that invalidated the earlier debt-service-capacity attempt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithConvexDistressThreshold
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), ADD(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))), INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0.15)))
considered.hypothesis: Distress costs are convex, not linear: being slightly more levered than peers is manageable, but once leverage exceeds the industry norm by a material margin the firm enters the region where covenants bind, lenders demand cash and accrual reversals must be settled immediately rather than absorbed.
considered.reasoning: This is a functional-form hypothesis about firms rather than an estimator swap: adding a kink at 15 percentage points of excess leverage tests whether the accrual-fragility interaction is threshold-driven, which is the economic explanation for the family's pattern of strong decile alphas alongside weak linear slopes. Unlike the earlier indicator gate that destroyed the alpha by zeroing half the cross-section, every firm retains its rank-based weight, so the portfolio tails stay populated while the slope gains the extra curvature.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsPerUnitOfLossAbsorbingCapital
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: What matters is the size of the accrual relative to the capital that must absorb its reversal: the same accrual-to-assets figure is trivial for a firm with a thick equity cushion and existential for one whose book equity has been eroded, so accruals scaled by loss-absorbing capital is itself the interaction.
considered.reasoning: Arithmetically this equals the accrual-to-assets ratio multiplied by the assets-to-equity leverage factor, so the fragility amplification is continuous and unbounded in the *level* of leverage rather than compressed into a [0,1] rank — a structurally different design from the ten multiplicative variants in the archive and the one most likely to produce a strong cross-sectional slope, since the amplification no longer discards magnitude information. Flooring the denominator at cash holdings keeps it positive for firms with negative or near-zero book equity, so the sign is well defined precisely where distress is most severe, and winsorising controls the remaining scale.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithProductMarketAndFinancialWeakness
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), SUMRANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))), IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that is losing revenue share to its peers *and* carrying more debt than they do faces fragility on two independent fronts — it cannot grow out of its accrued working capital and cannot refinance around it — so its accrual reversals are the least likely to be absorbed.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the collinear leverage blend the critic rejected, product-market decline and financial over-extension are conceptually and empirically distinct dimensions, and each independently produced the archive's strongest evidence in its own metric (sales gap: fmb −2.03; leverage gap: α −4.7%, t −3.48). Both legs are industry-demeaned, so neither the sector composition of leverage nor an industry-wide demand shock can drive the sort, and the SUMRANK multiplier stays smooth so the cross-sectional slope is not degraded.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithDemandLoss
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The damage from an accrual reversal is its size relative to the equity that must absorb it, and its likelihood is highest when the firm is losing revenue to peers, so the two should be measured multiplicatively: accrual per dollar of loss-absorbing capital, amplified by idiosyncratic demand loss.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two structurally different innovations — continuous, unbounded fragility scaling through the equity-cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, Sharpe −0.456) and the best-performing peer-relative conditioner — rather than adding a twelfth rank multiplier to the same asset-deflated accrual. If the combination beats both parents, it establishes that magnitude scaling and conditional amplification capture different aspects of fragility, which is the key open question for the final generation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithVolatileRevenueBase
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(sale, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Fragility can be operating rather than financial: a firm whose revenue base swings unpredictably cannot forecast the collections and inventory turnover its accruals presume, so accrued earnings in such firms are systematically less likely to convert to cash.
considered.reasoning: Leverage volatility worked as a second-moment conditioner (α −4.1%, t −3.03) but plausibly proxied for restructuring activity; revenue volatility isolates business risk with no financing content and shares no variable with the accrual leg, so it discriminates between the two interpretations of that result. It is the only untested fragility dimension that is a genuine second moment of the operating business.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BalanceSheetAccrualsWithDemandLoss
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Balance-sheet working-capital accruals are informative specifically when demand is deteriorating — that is when a rise in receivables and inventory cannot be explained by growth — which would explain why this accrual leg predicts correctly with revenue-based conditioners and perversely with financing-based ones.
considered.reasoning: The balance-sheet leg produced the archive's strongest slope with the within-firm revenue trough (fmb −3.63) but sign-flipped with chronic contraction (α +3.3%) and cash-flow coverage (α +0.7%), and this pins down whether the demand channel is what rescues it, using the conditioner form that has proven most reliable. It also carries the highest coverage in the archive (~0.10 versus 0.08), so a confirmation would give the final generation a broader-sample alternative to the cash-flow accrual leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithSlowCashConversionVsPeers
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(act, sale))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose current assets represent far more days of sales than its industry peers has a structurally slow cash conversion cycle, so accrued earnings sit in receivables and inventory for longer, are more exposed to obsolescence and non-collection, and cannot be turned into cash quickly when obligations fall due.
considered.reasoning: This replaces a threshold transplant with a new fragility dimension — the length of the operating cycle relative to peers — which is an operating-liquidity constraint rather than any of the financing, demand, or second-moment dimensions already tested, and it is a *level* measure so it is not mechanically tied to the accrual change in the other leg. Industry-demeaning is essential here because cycle length is a sector technology, and it is the transformation that has consistently improved this family's cross-sectional slopes.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsUnderWorstDimensionOfFragility
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), MAX(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
considered.hypothesis: Financial fragility is determined by the binding constraint, not by an average: a firm that is severely over-levered relative to peers is fragile even if its revenue is growing, and a firm losing revenue share is fragile even at modest leverage, so the relevant amplifier of accrual risk is the *worst* of the two peer-relative dimensions.
considered.reasoning: This is a functional-form hypothesis about how distress dimensions aggregate, and MAX is a structure the archive has never used — it directly contrasts with the SUMRANK average of the same two dimensions, so the pair identifies whether fragility is additive or determined by a single binding constraint. Because MAX keeps a firm in the extreme portfolios when either dimension is extreme, the short leg should be populated by genuinely stressed firms rather than by moderate cases that score middling on both, which is the plausible reason averaging has capped this family's alpha near −4.7%.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DualEstimateAccrualsWithDemandLoss
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(SUB(SUB(DELTA(act, 1), DELTA(che, 1)), SUB(DELTA(lct, 1), DELTA(dlc, 1))), dp), at)), 1), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: The cash-flow and balance-sheet accrual measures are two noisy estimates of the same economic quantity; their sum retains the common accrual signal while the estimation errors — articulation differences, mergers, reclassifications — partially cancel, so the extreme portfolios contain firms where both statements agree that accruals are extreme.
considered.reasoning: This directly repairs the sharpest anomaly in the archive: the balance-sheet leg with this conditioner gave fmb −3.90 but α −0.6%, exactly what happens when measurement noise widens cross-sectional dispersion without adding return information, while the cash-flow leg gave α −4.1% with fmb −2.03. Averaging the two estimates is an econometric fix with an economic justification, and it should inherit the slope strength of one leg and the portfolio strength of the other.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualsWithBindingNonDebtPressure
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), MAX(RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), sale))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))))))
considered.hypothesis: Financial pressure need not come from lenders: a firm financing itself with more payables and accrued expenses per sales dollar than its peers is already rationed, and combined with revenue share loss it is in the same weakest-link position as an over-levered firm.
considered.reasoning: Trade-credit dependence produced α −4.5% (t −3.61) as a standalone conditioner, close to peer leverage, so substituting it into the winning MAX structure tests whether the binding-constraint result is about debt specifically or about financing pressure generally — a substantive economic question, not a reshuffle. It also gives a robustness check on the gen-8 MAX finding using a conditioner drawn from an entirely different part of the balance sheet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CushionScaledAccrualsWithVolatileRevenue
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), MAX(ceq, che)), 1), RANK(VOL(RATIO(sale, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Fragility has a capacity dimension and an uncertainty dimension: a thin equity cushion determines how much of an accrual reversal the firm can absorb, while an unstable revenue base determines how likely the reversal is, so accruals scaled by loss-absorbing capital should be most damaging where revenue is least predictable.
considered.reasoning: Both ingredients worked independently through different channels — the cushion deflator (fmb −1.51, α −3.8%, Sharpe −0.456) and revenue-base volatility (fmb −1.65, α −3.7%) — and neither shares a variable with the other, so their combination tests whether absorption capacity and cash-flow uncertainty are complementary rather than duplicative descriptions of fragility. Unlike the peer-gap conditioners this pairing contains no growth or leverage term, so it provides an independent confirmation route for the family's central claim.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsCompositionAccrualsUnderExcessLeverage
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), ADD(ABS(ib), dp)), 1), RANK(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: What matters for a fragile firm is not how large accruals are relative to its asset base but what fraction of its reported earnings is non-cash: when most of the earnings of an over-levered firm is accrual rather than cash, there is nothing available to service obligations and the reported profit will not survive.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the fragile MAX(ceq, che) deflator with a strictly positive, scale-free earnings-composition denominator (|ib| + dp), so it measures earnings *quality* rather than accrual size — economically distinct from every asset-deflated leg in the archive and free of the near-zero-equity outlier risk the critic identified. Combined with the peer-relative leverage gap, the best-performing single conditioner (α −4.7%, t −3.48), it asks whether cash-poor earnings composition is the channel through which leverage amplifies accruals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CountOfBindingFragilityFronts
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), ADD(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0), ADD(INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(GROWTH(sale, 1))), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(che, lt))), 0))))
considered.hypothesis: Fragility accumulates discretely: each front on which a firm is worse than its industry norm — more levered, losing revenue share, holding less cash — removes one escape route from an accrual reversal, so the number of failed fronts, not the worst one, measures how trapped the firm is.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the degeneracy the critic identified: a maximum of three cross-sectional ranks piles up near unity and becomes a near-constant multiplier, whereas a count of industry-median breaches is spread across 0–3 with substantial mass in each bucket, so the conditioning actually discriminates. It is also an Ohlson-style discrete distress score rather than another continuous rank transform, giving a genuinely different aggregation hypothesis than either MAX or averaging.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicPeerExcessLeverageAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), oancf), at), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(lt, at)), 0), 3))
considered.hypothesis: One year of above-peer leverage can be a deliberate, reversible financing choice, but three consecutive years means the firm has been unable to deleverage and its debt capacity is exhausted, so accrual reversals must be absorbed by write-downs rather than by borrowing.
considered.reasoning: Rather than twisting the aggregation operator on two known legs, this introduces persistence on the archive's strongest conditioning dimension — a state variable distinct from its level (tested), its one-year change (tested) and its volatility (tested) — and the 0–3 count is well spread rather than compressed toward an endpoint. The economic claim is falsifiable and sharp: if only chronic excess leverage matters, this should beat the one-year peer gap; if the effect is about fresh deterioration, it should be weaker.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: A product of two all-positive ranks is monotone in each component and therefore loads mostly on the two well-known main effects (Sloan accruals and leverage/distress) rather than isolating any interaction, making it close to a repackaged rediscovery.

Construction is internally coherent — a signed balance-sheet accrual measure scaled by a strictly positive fragility rank preserves direction and genuinely amplifies rather than contaminates — though the core is still the classic Sloan accrual anomaly and the [0,2] multiplier provides only mild differentiation.

This is just the accrual anomaly with a different deflator (and the denominator double-counts cash, since che is inside act), so it tests a scaling choice rather than a cross-theme mechanism, with added small-denominator instability.

Accrual volatility (Dechow-Dichev/Francis accrual quality) interacted with leverage is a defensible cross-theme idea, but the sign is theoretically ambiguous (information-risk pricing implies positive premia), the rank product again absorbs both main effects, and the 5-period VOL on annual data will cut coverage.

The SUMRANK bundles a strong standalone profitability effect (−pi/at) with leverage change, so any result will most plausibly be driven by the well-documented profitability premium rather than the claimed accrual-under-funding-stress interaction, making attribution impossible.

Using a firm-relative TS_RANK of the current ratio gives a conditioner that is roughly uniform within firm and hence carries little unconditional return signal, making this the cleanest genuine interaction test in the batch, though the 5-period lookback and rank-product form still deserve scrutiny for coverage and main-effect leakage.

This is structurally the archive signal with a cosmetic swap of accrual proxy (ΔWC−dp → ib+dp−oancf, the textbook Hribar-Collins cash-flow accrual) and of the liquidity leg, and multiplying signed Sloan accruals by a strictly positive rank amplifier makes it a rescaled accruals anomaly whose sign already came out backwards (fmb +3.25 vs expected negative) in the prior test — the coverage fix does not address that diagnostic.

The double-demeaning is the right instinct for isolating a cross-derivative, but as a *univariate* sort/FMB signal the product conflates high-accrual/high-leverage firms with low-accrual/low-leverage firms in the same tail, whose expected returns move in opposite directions, so the stated negative sign does not follow from the expression without main-effect controls that this framework does not provide.

Using a within-firm leverage percentile as the conditioner genuinely prevents the cross-sectional leverage main effect from leaking in, which is the cleanest attribution among these proposals, though the [0,1] positive multiplier means the signal remains a shrunken re-scaling of the well-known accruals anomaly rather than an independent effect.

The sign is internally inconsistent with the accrual identity it invokes — a rise in taxes payable is an increase in current liabilities, i.e. a *negative* working-capital accrual that Sloan-type logic predicts precedes *higher* returns — and txp is sparsely and inconsistently reported, so coverage will likely be as thin as the archive signal it aims to fix.

The depreciation-lever channel is a genuinely distinct accrual-quality mechanism from working-capital accruals and the Altman-style conditioner avoids the profitability premium, but Δ(dp/at) is heavily contaminated by denominator growth and asset-mix/M&A changes, so a hit could simply be the asset-growth anomaly interacted with distress.

Substituting debt-maturity concentration for leverage level is the one conditioner change here that tests an economically different distress dimension (rollover pressure vs. solvency stock), giving a genuine contrast against Signal 1, though it still inherits the positive-multiplier design whose predictive content is dominated by the accrual leg.

This is a definitional swap on the archive's best portfolio signal — the conditioner is identical to AccrualsAtOwnLeverageHighWater and the accrual leg is essentially the gen-0 WorkingCapitalAccrualsFragilityAmplified leg (Δwcap−dp, refined to exclude cash and current debt) — so it functions as a coverage robustness check rather than a new mechanism, and the fact that the archive parent already had an FMB slope of the wrong sign (−1.27 vs. −3.13 alpha) is a diagnostic this variant does not address.

A legitimate additivity test crossing the archive's two strongest legs (ABS accruals, within-firm leverage peak) and internally consistent, but it is combinatorially derivative and the ABS×nonnegative-rank construction yields a one-sided, heavily skewed signal whose long-short spread will be driven almost entirely by an extreme-tail bucket rather than a monotone cross-sectional relation.

This is the most informative proposal in the set — it decomposes the archive's ABS-accrual alpha into its liquidation tail and constitutes a genuine sign-reversal test of Sloan inside the levered segment — though its validity hinges entirely on INDICATOR(x,0) firing on x>0 as assumed, and the resulting sample is a conditional subset (negative-accrual, high-leverage firms) whose effective breadth should be checked before interpreting the alpha.

The economic story (accruals building against a falling revenue base) is coherent and the expression matches it, but the stated attribution rationale is factually wrong — low sales growth is a long-documented standalone value/growth anomaly (Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny) and NEG(GROWTH(sale)) inside SUMRANK will import that main effect, so a positive result will be hard to separate from a known premium.

Receivable-component accruals conditioned on fragility is a reasonable parallel to the archive's inventory version, but it changes two things at once (component *and* deflator from at to sale), which breaks the very component-versus-generic attribution the proposal claims to deliver, and the underlying Δreceivables effect is itself a documented accrual-component result (Thomas–Zhang).

Substantively distinct conditioning dimension — a within-firm liquidity trough rather than a solvency peak — that is internally consistent, avoids the cross-sectional leverage main effect, and is paired with a controlled comparison that would genuinely identify which fragility state carries the interaction.

This is a pure accrual-proxy swap on an already-evaluated signal (AccrualsInFirmWorstRevenueYear, fmb −3.63 / ls_talpha −2.48) with the identical conditioner and identical mechanism, i.e. a cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different hypothesis, and the two accrual measures are highly collinear so it is unlikely to teach anything new.

The recch+invch aggregation paired with the within-firm revenue trough is a new and internally consistent cell (sign convention of the cash-flow-statement components is handled correctly by the NEG), and the stated attribution motive — isolating whether the earlier FMB weakness came from the conditioner or the component leg — is legitimate, though it remains an incremental recombination within a well-worked family and coverage near 0.07 is a real fragility.

The within-firm cash-to-total-liabilities trough is a genuinely distinct conditioning state from the archive's cross-sectional che/lct and TS_RANK leverage, the expression's direction matches the negative expected sign, and holding the accrual leg fixed makes it a clean controlled comparison — but replacing lct with lt is a modest change and the mechanism is close to the already-tested liquidity fragility idea.

This simply multiplies two already-evaluated conditioners together without a new economic mechanism, and because SUMRANK compresses the two TS_RANKs toward the middle the likely outcome is a diluted version of the stronger single-conditioner signal rather than the additive sharpening claimed — the "stacking distress dimensions" framing is a hypothesis about statistics, not about firms.

The funding-source-of-the-accrual mechanism is a genuinely new dimension relative to the archive's distress stocks and operating decline, the within-firm ranking is a defensible way to strip the known net-debt-issuance and asset-growth premia, and the expression direction matches the negative expected sign; the main caveat is mechanical correlation between DELTA(lt) and the accrual leg itself, which should be diagnosed if the signal works.

The one-sided restriction is well motivated by the archive's fmb +3.55 on the negative tail and gives real attribution value as the exact complement of an evaluated signal, but zeroing roughly half the cross-section leaves a large mass at zero that will make the long leg's composition arbitrary and can inflate or destroy ls_talpha for reasons unrelated to the hypothesis.

ZSCORE(RANK(·)) is a strictly monotone rescaling of the accrual leg, so this adds no new information relative to the already-evaluated AccrualsInFirmWorstRevenueYear, and the stated motivation ("weak Fama-MacBeth slopes") contradicts that parent's fmb_tstat of −3.63, which was already the family's strongest cross-sectional evidence.

The diagnosis of skew-driven FMB failure in ReceivableAccrualsInFragileFirms is honest and well-argued, but the fix is a monotone rank rescaling of the same measure with the same conditioner, i.e. a scale-level cosmetic variant rather than a substantively different hypothesis, and it will chiefly test regression mechanics rather than economics.

Industry-demeaning is not a monotone transform of the raw accrual and so genuinely changes the signal's information content (removing structural working-capital-cycle heterogeneity), giving a defensible measurement improvement over AccrualsAtOwnLeverageHighWater — though it sits close to the well-known industry/abnormal-accrual literature and reuses an already-tested conditioner.

ni−ib introduces a realised-distress dimension absent from the archive, the sign logic is internally consistent (RANK is non-negative so the product preserves the accrual direction), and the main caveat is the large mass point at ni=ib that will make the conditioner near-constant for most firms and concentrate identification in the loss tail — worth testing, but check coverage and rank ties.

Sharpening the debt-funded-accrual mechanism from total liability growth to the maturity of the incremental funding is an economically substantive refinement of the strongest new gen-3 dimension, it avoids mechanical overlap with the cash-flow accrual construction, and the within-firm TS_RANK conditioner keeps the debt-issuance and asset-growth premia out of the sort.

Multiplying two already-tested leverage conditioners (one of which produced essentially zero alpha) is a stacking variant that reweights rather than cleanly separates "level" from "deterioration"; a proper test of that distinction requires orthogonalising the within-firm leverage state against the cross-sectional level or a double sort, not a product of two [0,1] ranks that also thins the extreme portfolios.

The flow-based debt-service conditioner (oancf/lt) is a genuinely new and smoothly distributed dimension for this family, the sign logic matches the expression, and using the balance-sheet accrual leg sensibly avoids sharing oancf across legs — though the reviewer should watch whether the result is just the well-known cash-flow-to-debt/profitability effect leaking through the rank multiplier.

Mechanically consistent and sign-coherent, but it is simply the in-sample best accrual leg crossed with the in-sample best conditioner from the archive, i.e. a recombination selected on prior results rather than a new economic claim, and the low-coverage recch leg raises overfitting risk.

Replacing lt with lt−che inside the archive's existing leverage-above-own-norm conditioner is a marginal rescaling of the parent signal (net debt and gross debt above own norm will be highly correlated), so the test is unlikely to be economically informative relative to its cost.

Persistence-versus-trough is a defensible economic distinction and the expression matches the hypothesis, but the structure is a straight hybrid of two archive templates (loss-count SUMRANK and revenue-trough conditioning) and the 0–3 declining-year count is coarse, so expected incremental information is modest.

Working-capital accruals are a mechanical component of asset growth, so multiplying the accrual by NEG(GROWTH(at,1)) selects a thin, internally contradictory corner of the joint distribution and risks producing a partition of a single variable (and of the known asset-growth anomaly) rather than a true conditional effect.

Lagging the accrual leg of an existing archive signal while keeping the identical conditioner is a decay diagnostic, not a new mechanism, and with annual data plus reporting lag the accrual is roughly two years stale, where the accrual anomaly is known to be largely exhausted.

Rank-averaging two already-evaluated conditioners that both measure excess leverage (peer-relative and self-relative) is a near-collinear blend rather than a substantively new mechanism, and the archive gives no reason to expect a smoothed average of two ~-4.7% alpha variants to be more than a cosmetic reshuffle.

Book-tax divergence is a genuinely untested channel in this archive with a coherent interaction logic and a sensible firm-relative construction, though the reviewer should check that the tax-intensity deviation is not simply reproducing the already-tested "own-norm profitability decline" conditioners and that overlap with the published tax-to-book anomaly is acknowledged.

A legitimate and cleanly specified test of whether peer benchmarking (rather than leverage per se) is what makes the conditioner work, but it remains a one-variable substitution into a proven template with modest expected incremental information.

Pairing the strongest accrual component with the strongest conditioner is a mechanically obvious 2x2 recombination of previously evaluated ingredients, so it is worth one run as an independence check but carries low novelty and real coverage risk (~0.075).

Involuntary maturity shortening is economically distinguishable from new short-term borrowing and the construction matches the hypothesis, but dltt/lt deviations are arithmetically close to the already-tested dlc-based rollover conditioner, so the marginal information may be small.

The claim that dropping oancf removes mechanical overlap is wrong — pi is essentially pre-tax ib and dp appears in both legs — so the signal largely reduces to accruals interacted with (negative) industry-adjusted profitability, a conditioner dimension the archive has already probed with weak results.

The expression matches the hypothesis and the sign direction is correct, and since the revenue-decline conditioner produced the archive's strongest Fama-MacBeth slope the industry-demeaned version has a defensible diagnostic purpose — but it remains a third slice of an already-twice-tested conditioner dimension (own-norm, chronic-contraction, now peer-relative) and is close to a mechanical accruals×low-sales-growth double-anomaly stack.

This is essentially an estimator re-scaling of the archive's best signal (AccrualsWithLeverageAboveIndustryNorm, α −4.7%, t −3.48) with the accrual leg replaced by a within-industry percentile, and converting accruals to a bounded rank discards precisely the tail magnitude where accrual reversals are concentrated, so the "robustness" argument is a cosmetic rather than economic motivation.

The equity-cushion channel was already tested in own-norm form (AccrualsAsRetainedEarningsErode, α −4.3%, t −2.97) and the family now contains roughly ten interchangeable accruals×RANK(IND_ADJ(distress proxy)) variants all landing near α −3% with weak FMB support, so this predictable peer-relative rerun cannot resolve the family's central slope-versus-alpha disagreement.

Leverage *volatility* is a genuinely distinct second-moment conditioner rather than another level, trend or peer-gap rescaling, the expression is internally consistent with the stated sign, and a positive result would meaningfully reinterpret the family as being about financing unreliability — though the conditioner will load on small, restructuring and high-turnover firms and should be checked against a leverage-level control.

This is a legitimate one-leg ablation of ReceivableAccrualsInFragileFirms with correct recch sign convention and a clear attribution question, but it will be very highly correlated with the parent signal, so its informational value is diagnostic rather than exploratory and it should not be scored as a new mechanism.

Trade-credit dependence is a genuinely untested, non-debt pressure dimension and the construction is coherent, but the sign is theoretically two-sided — high payables per sales dollar also proxies for supplier bargaining power and operating-liability leverage, which the Nissim-Penman evidence links to *higher* profitability — and (lct − dlc) shares working-capital components with the accrual leg, so any result needs a bargaining-power control before interpretation.

The expression and hypothesis are consistent and the two industry-demeaned legs are conceptually distinct, but this is essentially a SUMRANK average of two already-tested conditioners on the identical accrual leg, so the most likely outcome is a result interpolating between the two parents rather than new economic information.

This is a cosmetic recombination — the gen-7 convex-threshold functional form transplanted onto the already-tested industry-relative sales-growth conditioner — and its stated motivation (fmb −1.76 vs −1.68 on the leverage version) is well inside noise, while the added indicator at a 0.10 industry-adjusted growth gap likely has thin mass and will barely perturb the rank multiplier.

Changing the accrual deflator to loss-absorbing capital is a substantive structural change rather than another rank multiplier, the hypothesis matches what the expression computes, and the sign is unambiguous; the main risk to watch is that the MAX(ceq, che) deflator concentrates the tails in tiny-equity firms, so the resulting spread should be checked for unstable portfolio composition despite the 1% winsorization.

Revenue-base volatility is a genuinely untested, purely operating second-moment conditioner that shares no variable with the accrual leg and cleanly discriminates between the financing and business-risk readings of the leverage-volatility result, though it edges toward the known finding that the accrual anomaly concentrates in high-uncertainty/high-arbitrage-risk firms and should be interpreted with that in mind.

This is an ablation of the already-evaluated ReceivableAccrualsInFragileFirms — one of its two SUMRANK legs dropped and che/lct swapped for che/lt — so while the decomposition is diagnostically sensible, as a standalone signal it is close to a rediscovery of an archived construction rather than a new mechanism.

Internally consistent and usefully diagnostic — it swaps the within-firm revenue-trough conditioner for the cross-sectional industry-relative one on the higher-coverage balance-sheet accrual leg — but it remains a straightforward recombination of two archived legs, and the growth conditioner risks importing a value/low-growth tilt that the FF5 alpha should be inspected for.

Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is a mechanical cross of two already-tested archive components (the MAX(ceq,che) deflator from gen 7 and the MAX-aggregated peer-gap amplifier from gen 8) with no new economic content, so it functions as a cosmetic stacking of prior winners rather than a substantively different mechanism — and the fragile MAX(ceq,che) deflator adds outlier risk when book equity is near zero or negative.

The construction is self-defeating: the maximum of three [0,1] cross-sectional ranks concentrates near unity for most firms, so the "amplifier" becomes nearly constant and the signal degenerates toward the plain Sloan accrual measure — the opposite of the claimed conditioning sharpening, and the stated benefit of "broadening the short leg" is really conditioning dilution.

This is the only proposal that changes the accrual measurement itself rather than reshuffling conditioners, and the Hribar–Collins-style articulation-error motivation is a legitimate diagnosis of the FMB-vs-alpha divergence between the two legs — though the hypothesis overstates the mechanism, since a sum is an average, not a conjunction, and can be extreme on one estimate alone.

Switching MAX to MIN on identical legs is an operator knob-twiddle whose outcome is largely inferable from the already-observed MAX (strong) versus SUMRANK-average (zero) results, and MIN of two ranks compresses the amplifier toward zero for nearly all firms, so any spread will be driven by a thin, unstable tail rather than the claimed conjunction economics.

Substituting trade-credit dependence for peer leverage in the MAX structure is a defensible economic test of whether the binding-constraint result is about debt or financing pressure generally, but the conditioner (lct − dlc)/sale overlaps mechanically with the payables component embedded in the accrual leg, so a positive result may partly reflect construction overlap rather than distinct fragility.

Coherent capacity-times-uncertainty story with an amplifier that shares no variable with the accrual leg, giving a genuinely independent confirmation route, but it is still a pairing of two previously tested components and risks proxying known earnings/sales-volatility and thin-equity (distress) effects rather than an accrual-reversal channel.
